SearchHow we decideRulings

Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Town, shops & places

exhibition noun

a public show of art or objects

also exhibitions, art exhibition, exhibit (a show), exposition, expo, show (of art)

modern

Levi–Bini p. 42

expositiō, expositiōnis f.

noun, third declension

an exhibition

Levi and Bini’s word, from expōnere, which Pliny uses of pictures put on show in public (Plin. NH 35.52: in pūblicō expōnī). Classically expositiō is a setting forth in words, a narration (Cic. Or. 212), and also the exposing of an infant (Lewis & Short), so say what is on show when there is any doubt (see exhibit).

Other words

  • spectāculum, spectāculī n. — a show, anything put on for people to see

    noun, second declension · also used · classical · Cic. Fin. 5.48: pompā, lūdīs atque ejus modī spectāculīs; Levi–Bini p. 25: spectāculum et pompa

    The general classical word for a show: games, a procession, a play, a sight (see scene, a sight).

  • exhibitiō, exhibitiōnis f.

    noun, third declension · avoid · modern · M-O s.v. museum (with a query, from Egger)

    Classically the producing of a document or a person, and maintenance, support (Gell. 14.2.7; the Digest; Lewis & Short); expositiō says “exhibition” without the legal sense.

Examples

  • Crās tabulās pictās quae in mūsēō prōpositae sunt vīsēmus.

    Tomorrow we’ll go and see the pictures on show at the museum.composed

See also exhibit, museum, picture, painter, scene.

SourcesLewis & Short: expositio · Lewis & Short: expono · Lewis & Short: spectaculum · Lewis & Short: exhibitio

Luigi Levi and Antonio Bini, Il latino come lingua viva (1937), pp. 25, 42; each word checked in Lewis & Short.

Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.v. museum.

Pliny checked against the Perseus Latin texts. Quotations from the Latinitas loci collections (loci-cicero-philosophica), checked against the editions named there.
